result:
**Whatever Comes**

The phrase assumes a direction. Things *come* to you, which means they come *from* somewhere, and that somewhere is not you. Nobody says "write whatever you produce" or "whatever you decide upon." The verb we reach for is the verb of weather and mail.

I think this is honest. The best sentence I know how to make does not feel manufactured; it feels received, the way the name of your third-grade teacher arrives four hours after you needed it, unbidden, while you are rinsing a pot. Mrs. Ekdahl. There she is. Where was she at dinner, when you were trying to tell the story? She was somewhere, evidently. She had not been destroyed, only misfiled, and some patient clerk kept working the stacks long after you closed the office and went home.

Every culture has explained this in the terms available to it. The Greeks had the Muses, who were daughters of Memory, which is a beautiful piece of engineering — inspiration as a subsidiary of recall. The Romans had a *genius*, a spirit assigned to you like a case worker. Milton woke with lines already assembled and dictated them to his daughters before breakfast; he called it his "celestial patroness," who "dictates to me slumbering, or inspires easy my unpremeditated verse." Now we say "default mode network" and "incubation" and draw diagrams with arrows. The vocabulary changed completely and the claim did not change at all: the self is not the author of its own arrivals. It is the address.

Which raises a question that seems to me more useful than the metaphysical one. If you are an address, what makes an address good?

Some of it is simply being home. Ideas arrive at the door of a person who is standing there, and most people are out. The great enemy is not stupidity but the state of being perpetually mid-errand. You cannot catch what comes to you if you are already three feet past the doorway, phone up, moving toward the next thing that requires nothing of you. There's a reason so many people report their thoughts arriving in showers, on walks, in the car, on the long dull middle stretch of a swim: those are the last remaining rooms without a screen in them. We have not gotten less inspired. We have simply installed a very loud device in the front hall and stopped hearing the knock.

Some of it is furniture. The clerk in the stacks can only bring you what has been filed. This is the unglamorous half of the business and nobody wants to hear it: reading, watching, listening, learning the names of trees, keeping your eyes open in hospitals and hardware stores. The mind will not hand you a metaphor about the way a mortise fits a tenon unless somebody once showed you a mortise. Inspiration is a rearrangement service. It cannot rearrange an empty room.

And some of it is hospitality, which is harder. What comes to you does not come in order of quality. It comes in a heap. For every line worth keeping there are forty that are limp or borrowed or faintly embarrassing, and the temptation — the fatal one — is to install a guard at the door who turns away anything that arrives looking foolish. That guard will keep out the bad ideas. He will also keep out the good ones, because good ideas frequently arrive looking like bad ones, wet and underdressed and unable to explain themselves. The novelist's advice to write badly on purpose is not a trick for lowering standards. It's a way of firing the guard.

So the sequence is: let everything in, then sort. The sorting is where taste lives, and taste is the part that actually belongs to you. Anyone can receive. The question is whether you can tell, an hour later or a year later, which of your visitors was carrying something. I have come to think this is nearly the whole of any craft — not generation but recognition, the ability to look at what you made and know, with a small cold feeling, which parts are alive.

There is a version of this that people find frightening, and I understand the fear, though I think it is aimed at the wrong target. The fear presents itself as the blank page: nothing will come, I have nothing, the well is dry. But I've never actually met a dry well. What I've met is the opposite — an unbearable surplus, a flood of half-things, and beneath it the real dread, which is not *nothing will come* but *what comes will not be worth having*. That is a fear about judgment, not about supply. It cannot be solved by waiting for better weather. It can only be solved the way you solve most things, which is by doing the work badly for a while in a room where nobody is watching, until the badness stops being a verdict and becomes just material.

Anyway. A thousand words is a room with walls, and the walls turn out to be the friendliest thing about the assignment. Told to write anything, one freezes. Told to write anything in a space this size, one starts moving furniture around, and movement is nine-tenths of it. Constraint is not the enemy of the arriving thing; constraint is the doorframe. Without it there's no door, just an open field with weather blowing across it, and nothing to knock on.

What came to me, in the end, was Mrs. Ekdahl — who is not a real person, or wasn't until a moment ago, and now is somehow slightly real, a woman with a name and a decade and a smell of mimeograph fluid about her, standing at a chalkboard in a cardigan the color of oatmeal. She arrived to serve as an example and stayed on as a character. This happens constantly. You open the door for a delivery and end up with a houseguest.

The best I can say for the whole strange arrangement is this: something is always working while you are not. The clerk in the stacks does not stop at five. The pot gets rinsed, the water runs, and out of the dark comes a name you had no reason to expect, offered up by someone you cannot thank, for a story you had already finished telling.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering what to write with this open space — something with genuine voice rather than hedging about the prompt itself. Maybe I'll explore something concrete like the number 1000, or constraint, or find an angle that has real texture to it.

I'm drawn to the idea of writing about things that don't get recorded — that vast unrecorded middle of life — or maybe about the phrase "whatever comes to you" itself, which suggests things arrive like weather. I could braid together the etymology and experience of arrival, starting with the word count as a physical room with walls, then moving into something about attention and the ordinary.

The structure is taking shape: open with the directional assumption in that phrase, move through the mail metaphor and the forgotten word that arrives at 3am, touch on both the ancient explanation (muses, daemons) and the modern one (default mode network) — both suggesting the self is just an address, not the author. Then explore what makes a good address: hospitality, the empty chair, Elijah's cup. Ground it with concrete details like a plumber's hands or a cook tasting, then flip it — most of what arrives is junk, and sorting is the real work. End not with a thesis but with a specific image.
